---
name: browser-automation
description: Use browser automation to inspect or interact with websites, test rendered interfaces, capture screenshots, and diagnose console or network behavior.
---

# Browser Automation

Use these tools for rendered state, authentication, interaction, accessibility,
layout, screenshots, console output and network traffic.

OpenCode exposes `browser_help` and `browser_dispatch`; Codex namespaces `help`
and `dispatch` under this plugin. First call help without an action to discover
available names; use only listed actions. Help also loads one argument schema.
Dispatch takes `{ "action": "navigate_page", "arguments": { "url": "https://example.com" } }`.
Put every action field inside `arguments`. Load help when a signature is unclear.
Direct action tools, when present, use the same workflow. `batch` is compact-only.

The host supplies conversation identity. Never add routing fields. Codex
subagents share their parent's tabs; coordinate using explicit `page` handles.

1. Reuse the current page. Open `new_page` only for simultaneous work (default cap 5), and close temporary pages when done. New pages default to background.
2. Inspect before acting. `take_snapshot` supports `find`, `within` a UID, `interactive`, `diff`, and `maxLines` (default 300, maximum 2000). Search or scope large pages instead of repeatedly requesting the full tree. Diff cannot be combined with filters.
3. Copy UIDs exactly. They include a worker prefix; refresh after navigation, worker replacement or missing elements. File exports are diagnostic dumps with upstream UIDs; obtain actionable UIDs from an inline snapshot.
4. Prefer `fill_form` for several inputs: `arguments: {"elements":[{"uid":"<snapshot UID>","value":"text"}]}`. Values are strings; use the displayed option text for selects. Load help before guessing other argument shapes. Use `batch` for up to 8 already-understood steps, with a snapshot only on the last step. It stops on error; inspect completed/not-run counts and never replay a partially completed batch blindly.
5. Verify the observable result. A successful tool call alone does not prove the intended effect. Input actions omit snapshots unless requested; inspect when the result matters. When the visible confirmation supplies the requested facts, stop. An order ID and total in a confirmation are receipt data; a separate page labelled "Receipt" is unnecessary. Use `wait_for` for an expected change, not a guessed extra section or success screen.

`list_pages` shows session-local `p1`, `p2`, etc. `select_page` changes current;
`page` on scoped actions targets an owned page without changing current. Unknown
or closed handles fail. Selecting does not focus the window unless requested.

Scroll with `press_key` (`PageDown`, `PageUp`, `Home`, `End`). Use screenshots for visual work. Console and network lists default to 50 entries;
paginate or narrow them. Export large request/response bodies to workspace files.
Text responses are bounded to 32 KiB; truncation is explicit. Images remain intact.

For login or other user work, `handoff` start focuses the exact headed page and
pauses automation on it. End the turn and request the user's work. Finish only
after confirmation, then take a fresh snapshot. Other owned pages remain usable.

`status` observes without launching a browser or worker. CLI `doctor` diagnoses
configuration. Ordinary action errors retain healthy workers; interrupted actions
may have happened and are never replayed automatically.

`fill_secret`, when configured, accepts a secret name and input UID; it checks an
allowed HTTPS top-level origin and returns no value. Do not read the filled value.
Recording tools appear only when explicitly enabled; stop recordings before
cleanup. There is no automatic capture, HAR export, or rolling recorder.

# Browser MCP

[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@mirsella/browser-mcp)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@mirsella/browser-mcp)
[![CI](https://github.com/mirsella/browser-mcp/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/mirsella/browser-mcp/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

One shared browser profile with separate tab ownership for OpenCode sessions
and Codex conversations. The plugin wraps
[`chrome-devtools-mcp`](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp)
and routes each conversation through its own browser tabs while sharing cookies,
logins, local storage, cache, and extensions.

Package 2.x targets OpenCode v2 (2.0.27 or newer). Package 1.x retains the
OpenCode v1 adapter (1.18 or newer, below 2). Codex uses the same Rust MCP
server and manifests in both releases. The native v2 adapter uses
`@opencode/plugin`; local directories also expose a physical `server` entrypoint.

Install `@mirsella/browser-mcp` for OpenCode v2, or `@mirsella/browser-mcp@opencode1`
for OpenCode v1. Existing Nix-managed and local-directory installations can keep
their configured paths.

## Requirements

- OpenCode 2.0.27 or newer, or Codex with plugin and hook support
- Linux x64
- Bun
- A local Chromium-family browser
- A graphical session, unless `OPENCODE_BROWSER_HEADLESS=true`

## OpenCode setup

Add the plugin to `opencode.json`. It enables the browser server and makes
the browser automation skill available by default:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/v2/config.json",
  "plugins": ["@mirsella/browser-mcp"]
}
```

Restart OpenCode after changing its configuration. That is the complete setup.
You do not need a separate installation, broker command, or background service.

The first adapter starts the packaged native broker automatically.
Concurrent Codex and OpenCode instances converge on the same private socket and browser
profile. The broker remains available while at least one adapter is connected,
then closes the browser and exits shortly after the final adapter disconnects.

The CDP port defaults to `9222`. If that port is occupied, the broker logs the
collision and selects a free loopback port without adopting or stopping the
other listener. Adapters keep the same configuration and share the selected
endpoint. A replacement broker also reconnects a restarted profile owner when
its Unix UID, profile argument and actual loopback socket ownership match.
Chromium's flattened process titles additionally require an open file under
that profile. A changed browser generation clears old tab ownership; unrelated
listeners and browsers without a previously trusted generation are not adopted.

OpenCode loads the JavaScript `./server` package export. Codex uses the
plugin and MCP manifests plus the session hooks. Both integrations launch
the same packaged Rust executable.

## Timeouts and diagnostics

Each browser action has one deadline for catalog discovery, browser startup,
session locking, execution, and reconciliation. `OPENCODE_BROWSER_OPERATION_SECONDS`
sets that deadline and defaults to 540 seconds. Catalog discovery and compact
help have a separate 70-second limit. A failed or panicking catalog discovery
can be retried without restarting the broker.

After an interrupted action, the next call replaces that session's worker and
reconciles its existing owned tabs. Actions are never replayed automatically.
Dispatched tab creation finishes registering ownership or closing that exact
target after caller cancellation. Inspect the page before retrying a write
because it may already have taken effect.

The broker writes diagnostics to
`$XDG_STATE_HOME/browser-mcp/broker-<profile-hash>.log`, or
`~/.local/state/browser-mcp/` when `XDG_STATE_HOME` is unset. Its startup message
prints the exact path. Logs are readable only by your user and also go to stderr.

Request tracing records the tool name, session ID, current stage, and elapsed
time. Chrome DevTools worker stderr is drained into that private broker log,
so replacement workers survive a disconnected host's stderr. Request tracing
does not record tool arguments. If a call stalls, look for its last
stage and whether the broker recorded a deadline, cancellation, catalog failure,
or worker replacement. Browser stderr is captured in
`browser-<profile-hash>.log` in the same directory. Its separate writer survives
broker replacement and exits when Chromium closes the pipe. Each broker or
browser log retains an 8 MiB file and one rotated `.log.1` backup. A browser that
exits during startup reports that exit immediately.

## Codex setup

The release tarball contains the executable, both integrations, and a local
Codex marketplace. Download it from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/mirsella/browser-mcp/releases),
extract it to a permanent directory, then register that directory:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add /path/to/browser-mcp
codex plugin add browser@browser-mcp
```

The npm package is now `@mirsella/browser-mcp`; it replaces `@mirsella/opencode-browser-mcp`.
To use a GitHub release in OpenCode, set the plugin entry to the `file:///absolute/path`
of its unpacked directory instead of the npm name.

For a source checkout, build and stage the binary first (`bun run build:native`
and `bun run stage:native`). Use a packaged directory for installation so
compiler outputs are not copied into Codex's plugin cache.

The installed plugin is enabled by default. Open `/hooks` in Codex to review
and trust its two hooks, then restart Codex. They inject the conversation ID
before browser calls and release owned tabs at `SessionEnd`. Browser calls
without an injected identity fail closed. The plugin exposes compact `help`
and `dispatch` tools and loads the same browser automation skill as OpenCode.

Codex and OpenCode use separate ownership namespaces while sharing the existing
broker, profile, cookies and logins. Codex's hook API identifies subagents with
their parent conversation ID, so subagents share that conversation's tabs.
Use separate pages when they work concurrently.

Codex runs `SessionEnd` on normal shutdown, on archive/delete of an open
conversation, or after 30 minutes idle with no client connected. Its hook has
a three-second deadline: the broker acknowledges cleanup promptly, then waits
for active calls before closing only that conversation's owned tabs. Cleanup
does not start a broker when none is running. Crashes still use normal broker
shutdown and idle cleanup.

The Codex MCP entry uses a 540-second tool timeout. Add `--direct-tools` to its
arguments when configuring per-action Codex tool approval rules; compact
dispatch has one approval rule for all actions.

## Plugin behavior

The plugin:

- registers and enables the packaged browser MCP adapter;
- injects the active OpenCode session ID after model argument generation;
- exposes compact browser tools unless existing permissions require direct tools;
- releases owned tabs when an OpenCode session is deleted;
- registers the bundled browser automation skill when the server is enabled.

The adapter preserves OpenCode's MCP request metadata and routes calls by
`_meta["ai.opencode/sessionID"]`, including calls that bypass the plugin tool
hook. Legacy plugin routing and Codex hooks remain supported. Conflicting or
missing identities fail closed; unidentified callers never share a browser
session. The broker still binds each session to its original workspace and
keeps tab ownership separate.

OpenCode sees two compact tools by default:

- `browser_dispatch` executes one browser action.
- `browser_help` lists actions or loads one action schema.

If the plugin detects per-action `browser_*` permission or tool rules, it uses
direct tools so those policies continue to work.

Settings:

- `enabled` (default `true`): start the server and load the skill. Set it to
  `false` to disable both. An explicit `mcp.servers.browser` entry takes precedence.
- `compactTools` (default `true`): keep `browser_dispatch` and `browser_help`
  instead of the direct tools. Set it to `false` to always use direct tools:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/v2/config.json",
  "plugins": [
    { "package": "@mirsella/browser-mcp", "options": { "compactTools": false } }
  ]
}
```

## Agent workflow and context

The initial MCP catalog remains two tools. Help returns one short signature and
argument schema. Structured upstream data is validated internally, then the
agent receives one readable copy plus any images. Text is limited to 32 KiB with
an explicit truncation notice. Network and console lists default to 50 entries.

- `list_pages` exposes stable session-local handles such as `p1`. `select_page`
  changes current; optional `page` on scoped actions targets another owned page
  without changing current. Closed handles fail rather than selecting another tab.
- `take_snapshot` adds `find`, `within`, `interactive`, `diff`, and `maxLines`
  (default 300, maximum 2000). Search includes ancestors. Diff requires compatible
  document/worker/verbosity state; an unavailable baseline is explicitly reported
  and replaced with a bounded full view. Baselines use at most 2 MiB per session.
- Inline snapshot UIDs include a worker namespace. Old-worker references fail
  before execution. Saved snapshot files retain upstream UIDs and are diagnostic
  exports; obtain actionable references from an inline snapshot.
- Compact-only `batch` runs up to 8 known actions under one session lock and
  deadline. All arguments, explicit pages and existing UIDs are checked first.
  Only the final step may return a snapshot. It stops on the first error and
  reports completed/not-run counts. Actions are never replayed automatically.
- `handoff` with `mode: "start"` focuses an exact headed page for user work and
  returns immediately. End the turn, request the user's work, then finish only
  after confirmation. Automation on that page pauses and normal idle cleanup is
  delayed for at most 24 hours. Explicit session release still closes owned tabs.
- `status` observes existing state without starting a browser or worker.
  `browser-mcp doctor` checks local configuration without starting services.

Ordinary action errors retain a healthy, reconciled worker and its element
references. Transport failures, interrupted calls and failed reconciliation still
replace the worker. New pages default to background; per-session window placement
may briefly activate an existing anchor window.

Recording is explicitly enabled with `--recording` or
`OPENCODE_BROWSER_RECORDING=true`. It requires `ffmpeg`; `--ffmpeg` or
`OPENCODE_BROWSER_FFMPEG` selects its executable. Only then do `screencast_start`
and `screencast_stop` appear. Artifacts are assigned under the conversation
workspace's `.scratch/browser-mcp/`. Stop recording before cleanup. Worker loss
can leave an incomplete file. Recordings use WebM. The encoder launcher rounds
padding to even dimensions to fix the pinned recorder's odd-viewport failure;
recording operations stop waiting after 30 seconds and report an incomplete
recording. There is no automatic or rolling capture.

Optional `--secrets-file` / `OPENCODE_BROWSER_SECRETS_FILE` enables `fill_secret`.
The existing file must be a same-user, nonsymlink, regular file with mode `0600`,
at most 64 KiB. No store is created. Its format is:

```json
{"account_password":{"value":"example-placeholder","origins":["https://example.com"]}}
```

Each name has a nonempty single-line value up to 4096 bytes and exact HTTPS
origins. `fill_secret` takes a name, an editable inline-snapshot UID and optional
page handle. It checks the top-level origin in the same synchronous function as
insertion and returns no value. Treat recordings and exported artifacts as
sensitive; see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

HAR export is deferred: the current worker does not expose the timing data needed
for an accurate HAR. Use paginated network lists and `get_network_request` with
`requestFilePath` / `responseFilePath` for focused diagnostics instead.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    O1[OpenCode instance A] --> A1[packaged stdio adapter]
    O2[OpenCode instance B] --> A2[packaged stdio adapter]
    A1 -->|private Unix socket| R[auto-managed broker]
    A2 -->|private Unix socket| R
    R --> T[CDP target tracker]
    R --> W[session worker pool]
    W --> C[chrome-devtools-mcp]
    T --> B[managed browser]
    C --> B
    B --> P[shared locked profile]
```

The adapter starts the broker on demand but does not own it. This lets adapters
from separate OpenCode processes share one browser without tying its lifetime to
whichever process connected first. Socket and profile locks make simultaneous
startup race-safe and prevent two browsers from opening the same profile.

Each routed session leases its own `chrome-devtools-mcp` worker. Stable
browser-level CDP target IDs remain the ownership authority; worker-local page
numbers are removed from model-visible schemas and responses.

## Ownership guarantees

- A tab has at most one owner.
- Routed sessions execute concurrently through separate workers.
- Popups inherit the owner of their opener tab.
- A session cannot select, inspect, or close another session's tabs through the broker.
- Manual and otherwise unowned tabs are not claimed during cleanup.
- Ownership conflicts, stale browser generations, and malformed responses fail closed.

These are routing guarantees, not an operating-system security boundary. Any
process running as the same Unix user can connect directly to the browser's
loopback CDP port.

## Browser and profile

The plugin detects Chromium, Google Chrome, Helium, Brave, and Microsoft Edge.
Chromium is preferred by default; `OPENCODE_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` overrides
automatic detection.
Google Chrome 136 and newer ignore remote-debugging flags for its default data
directory, so Chrome uses a dedicated directory under
`~/.config/opencode-browser-mcp` by default. Other detected browsers retain their
existing profile defaults.

The broker starts Chromium lazily on the first browser action. For a headed
browser it passes only a fixed allowlist of display and desktop variables. The
current process environment stays authoritative; missing values are recovered
from the current user session when available.

Configuration variables inherited from either host (the existing names are
shared by both integrations):

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` | auto-detected | Chromium-family executable |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_PROFILE` | browser-dependent | Shared browser data directory |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_HEADLESS` | `false` | Run without a visible window |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_SESSION_LAYOUT` | `shared-window` | `shared-window` or `window-per-session` |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_CDP_PORT` | `9222` | Preferred loopback CDP port; a free port is selected on collision |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_IDLE_MINUTES` | `30` | Fallback cleanup for routed sessions |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_MAX_PAGES` | `5` | Max owned tabs per agent session |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_STARTUP_SECONDS` | `20` | Browser startup deadline |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_OPERATION_SECONDS` | `540` | Browser operation deadline |
| `OPENCODE_BROWSER_DOWNSTREAM_COMMAND` | `bunx` | DevTools MCP launcher |

## Lifecycle

| Event | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| First adapter connects | One internal broker acquires the socket and profile leases |
| Tools are listed | Chromium remains stopped |
| First browser action | Chromium and the ownership tracker start |
| OpenCode turn becomes idle | Owned tabs remain available for the next turn |
| OpenCode session is deleted | Only that session's owned tabs close |
| Each session owns at most 5 pages | `new_page` beyond the cap fails; reuse a page with `navigate_page` or free one with `close_page` |
| Routed session reaches the configured inactivity timeout | Fallback cleanup closes that session's owned tabs; defaults to 30 minutes and `0` disables it |
| Another OpenCode instance connects | It shares the broker and profile with isolated tab ownership |
| Final adapter disconnects | The broker waits briefly, closes Chromium, and exits |
| Browser exits, segfaults, or is killed | The next browser action starts Chromium again; ownership from the old browser generation is discarded |
| DevTools worker exits or loses its transport | The next call replaces the worker and restores routing to surviving owned tabs |
| Broker exits unexpectedly | Connected adapters stay available and start one replacement on the next call; surviving tabs are restored only when the exact browser generation matches |
| MCP adapter exits unexpectedly | The OpenCode plugin reconnects it automatically, with retries up to 30 seconds apart |

Calls interrupted after dispatch can have taken effect. They return an error and
are never replayed automatically. Inspect the browser state before retrying an
action. Explicitly disabled or disconnected MCP entries stay disabled.

## Troubleshooting

- A headed startup error mentioning `DISPLAY` or `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` means no graphical session could be found. Set `OPENCODE_BROWSER_HEADLESS=true` when running without one.
- A profile or socket lease error means another live package process owns it or a stale process is still running. Do not bypass the locks.
- If startup reports that the profile is already open in another local process, that browser may have been opened without remote debugging. Save your work, close it gracefully, and retry the MCP action. MCP will start the same profile with remote debugging enabled. To leave that browser running, use a separate `OPENCODE_BROWSER_PROFILE` or `--profile` instead. Never delete Chromium's `SingletonLock` or kill the existing browser automatically.
- A process on the configured CDP port must belong to the exact managed browser generation. Stop it or choose another port.
- If downstream startup fails, verify that `bunx` is available to OpenCode.
- The plugin refuses to replace an unrelated `mcp.servers.browser` entry.

## Security

All sessions deliberately share cookies, authentication, storage, extensions,
permissions, history, and downloads. Browser content remains untrusted and may
contain prompt injection. The private same-UID socket prevents access by other
local users, but it does not isolate processes already running as your Unix user.

File exports can use the conversation's workspace and `/tmp/opencode`.
Chrome DevTools also permits its OS temporary directory. `/tmp/opencode`
is a shared scratch directory for small, temporary snapshots,
screenshots, and network responses. Clean up exported files when finished;
store larger or lasting artifacts in the workspace.

Read [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md) before using a profile with sensitive data.

## Development

```sh
cargo fmt --check
cargo test --all-targets
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
bun test tests/plugin.test.ts
cargo test --release --test e2e -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

The headed E2E starts adapters against temporary profiles, sockets, and CDP
ports. It checks automatic startup, startup races, cookie sharing, tab isolation,
concurrent calls, active-call cleanup, reconnect grace, compact
dispatch, both window layouts, and automatic browser shutdown.

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `plugin/` | OpenCode registration, session routing, and cleanup controls |
| `vendor/` | packaged native binary used directly by the OpenCode plugin |
| `src/broker.rs` | adapter bridge, managed broker lifecycle, routing, and leases |
| `src/cdp.rs` | stable CDP target tracking and ownership |
| `src/main.rs` | browser supervision, workers, and response filtering |
| `src/persistence.rs` | atomic generation-scoped ownership state |
| `tests/e2e.rs` | startup, shared-profile, isolation, routing, and shutdown coverage |

See [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the development and release workflow.

## Releases

CI builds and tests the distributable tarball on every push. Run the `release`
workflow from `main` with the full tested source commit: `main` for 2.x, or
`release/opencode-v1` for 1.x. The workflow verifies that commit and downloads
its checksummed CI artifact instead of rebuilding it. Dispatch with
`npm_mode=publish` to publish through npm's OIDC trusted publisher, create the
GitHub release, and update the Codex marketplace branch for `latest`. Use
`npm_mode=dry-run` to verify without writing. The channels are `latest` for 2.x
and `opencode1` for 1.x.

# Contributing

Contributions should preserve the ownership model rather than working around
it in an adapter or response filter.

## Requirements

- Rust 1.89 or newer
- Bun
- Node.js 20.19+, 22.12+, or 23+ for npm packaging
- A compatible headed Chromium-family browser for the E2E test
- A display server or Xvfb for headed browser tests
- `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` for the published native binary

## Checks

Run the normal checks before opening a pull request:

```sh
cargo fmt --check
cargo test --all-targets
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
bun test tests/plugin.test.ts
```

Run the real-browser test for changes to routing, ownership, browser startup,
cleanup, persistence, profile locking, or process shutdown:

```sh
cargo test --release --test e2e -- --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

For a headless Linux terminal, wrap the real-browser command in `xvfb-run -a`
to exercise headed handoffs and window placement. The compact workflow case
covers tab selection, UID lifetime, filtered snapshots, diffs, batch failure
boundaries and human handoffs. `actions::tests::context_budgets_and_pinned_schema_dialect`
prints static schema/help byte counts; these are not model-success measurements.
The public pinned tool-schema fixture comes from Chrome DevTools MCP 1.6.0.

The real-browser cases share Bunx's installation cache and run serially. Adapter
and tool-call concurrency is exercised within each case.

The E2E test starts adapters with temporary profiles, private sockets, and CDP
ports. It verifies automatic race-safe broker startup, shared cookies, tab
isolation, compact dispatch, concurrent calls, release during an active call,
reconnecting adapters, unowned-tab preservation, lazy Chromium activation,
per-session window placement, and automatic browser shutdown. The regular
integration suite verifies that one adapter disconnect cannot stop a broker
still used by another adapter.

Check the npm artifact when changing package files or the native binary:

```sh
rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
npm pack --dry-run
```

## Design rules

- Stable browser-level CDP tab target IDs are the ownership authority.
- Worker-local numeric page IDs are disposable routes and must not reach models.
- A tab can have only one browser session owner.
- Existing or unowned tabs must not be claimed by inference.
- Cleanup closes only exact targets owned by the retiring session.
- Browser generation changes invalidate ownership instead of guessing.
- Ownership conflicts and malformed downstream responses fail closed.
- One auto-managed broker owns the browser configuration, profile lease, socket
  lease, workers, and browser lifecycle.
- The first adapter starts the broker. Concurrent startup must converge on the
  lease winner rather than clone a browser or profile.
- Independent adapters may share one broker and profile. Their tab ownership
  remains isolated while browser profile data is shared deliberately.
- A second broker must fail clearly rather than share or clone an active profile
  or socket.
- Compact OpenCode tools disclose one current action schema at a time without
  duplicating upstream definitions.
- Per-action OpenCode permission or tool rules force direct mode rather than
  silently broadening access through the compact dispatcher.
- Tool discovery and compact help must not activate the browser runtime.
- The broker exits only after every adapter disconnects and the reconnect grace
  expires.
- Broker shutdown must reject new calls and give active calls up to five seconds
  to finish before closing workers and the browser.
- Window layout is best-effort presentation. Stable target ownership remains
  authoritative, and layout repair must not move, claim, or close tabs.

## Model browser evaluation

`scripts/browser-model-eval.ts` provides a local dummy shop, a transparent MCP
trace adapter, prompts, configuration, and an independent scorer. It exercises
a 221-product catalog, popup details, form entry, discount arithmetic, and a
checkout that fails its first valid submission. No money or external account
is involved. `bun test tests/model-eval.test.ts` checks the fixture's rejection
and retry behavior.

Use a fresh `.scratch/` directory per experiment. Record the source commit,
binary checksum, browser version, provider, exact model, and reasoning
setting. For source comparisons, give each checkout its own Cargo build
directory and reuse the shared Kache cache. Keep each condition's browser
skill.

Start `bun scripts/browser-model-eval.ts site --root=<root> --port=0` under a
known PID or held lock. Its `site.json` records the listening URL and PID. The
browser origin exposes no scoring endpoint. The host scorer reads order state
from files in the experiment directory; agents must not read those files.

Run names have a condition label and seed, such as `ours-current-1`,
`ours-guidance-2`, or `browser-use-1`. Seeds 1 and 2 select paired fixture
cases. Generate temporary project configuration with `config --root=<root>
--labels=ours-current,ours-guidance --condition=ours-guidance --seed=1
--ours-current=<binary> --ours-guidance=<binary>`. Merge it without
overwriting existing configuration. Each run gets its own profile and an
allocated CDP port. Restore the configuration and collect the fixture process
when finished.

For browser-use 1.0.0, install `browser-use==1.0.0` in a task-local Python
virtual environment. Keep the interpreter's virtual-environment path; do not
resolve its symlink. Write a JSON argv array containing that Python
executable, `scripts/browser-use-eval.py`, `--profile`, a fresh profile path,
`--ipc`, and a short task-local IPC path. Pass its path as
`--command=<argv.json> --backend=browser-use` to `config` or `mcp`.
External-command configurations require `--seed=1` or `--seed=2` to avoid
sharing one profile between active trials. The wrapper runs the official MCP
implementation with local headless Chromium and explicitly stops its browser.
Use a separate command file and profile for each seed. This dependency is for
evaluation only and is not part of the published server.

Generate each task with `prompt --root=<root> --run=ours-guidance-1
--port=<fixture-port> --skill=<condition-skill>`. Omit `--skill` for a server
that supplies its own packaged instructions. Page JavaScript, DOM operations
and normal page requests through the assigned browser MCP are permitted for
every condition. Host file/network access, fixture implementation (including
inline script contents), scoring data and other tools are forbidden. A
code-based server may use host code to orchestrate its browser helpers and
process observed page data, but cannot use it as a shortcut to the fixture's
private state.

Use separate model conversations with the same provider, model, reasoning,
harness and budgets. Counterbalance condition order across seeds. Compare the
current and candidate guidance on the same server binary before attributing
any difference to a runtime change. Test multi-harness routing separately from
single-agent task quality.

Save final answers to `<root>/answers.json` as objects containing `run`,
`answer`, `elapsedSeconds`, `thread`, optional provider `usage`, and `valid`.
Set `valid: true` only after inspecting the agent trace for forbidden tools,
source or oracle access. Run `score --root=<root>
--runs=ours-current-1,ours-guidance-1,browser-use-1`. A passing score requires
that audit, a complete trace of issued tool calls within the 50-call and
10-minute budgets, one correct order, all facts, and matching receipt data.
Setup failures and unaudited trials do not establish reliability.

The adapter records run identities independently of tool names and navigation,
so Python `browser_exec` calls and compact `dispatch` calls use the same
scorer. Reports include tool responses, client request bytes, initialization
and catalog response bytes, images, errors and supplied provider usage. Byte
counts are not tokens or billing. Include task/skill inputs and provider
token/cache/reasoning usage when available; do not infer total context or cost
from response bytes. Two paired cases are a smoke test, not a statistical
reliability estimate.

## Releases

Push the versioned source commit to `main` for 2.x, or to
`release/opencode-v1` for 1.x, and wait for CI. Dispatch `release.yml` from
`main` with the full source `commit` SHA. It verifies the pinned workflow and
source branch, then reuses the checksummed `npm-package` artifact.

Configure npm's trusted publisher as this repository's `release.yml` without
an environment. Dispatch with `npm_mode=publish` to publish through OIDC,
create the GitHub release, and update the Codex marketplace branch for `latest`.
Use `npm_mode=dry-run` to verify without writing. Versions 1.x use `opencode1`;
2.x use `latest`. GitHub releases attach the same tested tarball and
`SHA256SUMS`. Keep npm, Cargo and Codex versions synchronized.

CI runs headed tests against Chrome for Testing 155.0.8059.39. Update the pin
when validating a new browser version.

# Security policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please use [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/mirsella/browser-mcp/security/advisories/new).
Do not open a public issue for a vulnerability that exposes browser data,
credentials, local files, or cross-session tabs.

Include the package version, browser and version, MCP host, reproduction steps,
and whether the issue also reproduces with `chrome-devtools-mcp@1.6.0` directly.

## Security boundary

This project isolates tab ownership between cooperating MCP sessions. It is not
a sandbox for mutually untrusted local users or processes.

The broker keeps its Unix socket, profile lock, and ownership state private to
the current Unix user, but the managed browser exposes an unauthenticated CDP
endpoint on loopback. Any process running as the same user can connect to that
port and control the browser without going through the ownership broker.

Only one broker may open a given browser profile. The profile and socket locks
prevent accidental concurrent use and profile corruption; they are not a
security boundary against another process running as the same user. Multiple MCP
adapters are expected to connect to that broker and share its browser profile.

The broker socket accepts only peers with the broker's Unix UID and is created
with mode `0600` in a private directory. This protects against other local users,
not against another process already running as the same user.

All browser sessions share one user-data directory. This includes cookies,
authentication, local storage, cache, extensions, permissions, history, and
downloads. A session cannot inspect another session's tabs through the broker,
but websites can still communicate through shared browser data and origins.
The optional per-session window layout is visual organization only and does not
create another security boundary.

Browser content is untrusted input. Pages can include text designed to alter an
agent's behavior. The broker validates structured output internally before formatting bounded
model-facing text, but it cannot prevent prompt injection.

## Operational guidance

- Use a dedicated browser user-data directory for sensitive automation.
- Do not bypass or remove the profile or socket locks to run another broker.
- Let the packaged adapters share the auto-managed broker through its private
  socket. Do not start another browser against the same profile.
- Do not expose the CDP port beyond loopback.
- Do not run untrusted local processes while a sensitive profile is open.
- Use OS, container, or VM isolation when local users or workloads do not trust each other.
- Keep OpenCode, the browser, this package, and `chrome-devtools-mcp` updated.
- Review browser downloads and file writes before opening or executing them.
- Treat screenshots, DOM text, console messages, and network responses as untrusted data.

The downstream worker runs with usage statistics and CrUX requests disabled.
It also disables update checks and redacts headers that upstream classifies as
sensitive. The broker also masks common sensitive-name URL parameters, headers,
JSON/form fields, and configured secret values in model-facing network output.
This is heuristic redaction, not a guarantee that arbitrary secrets are removed.
Exported files, screenshots, recordings, DOM evaluation and unexpected encodings
can reveal values. These settings do not disable browser telemetry or prevent websites from
making network requests.

## Optional secrets and recordings

Secrets are loaded only from an explicitly configured, bounded, private file.
Insertion requires an exact allowed HTTPS top-level origin and editable element.
Origin checks and insertion run together; there is no origin check followed by a
separate navigation-sensitive insertion. Pages on an allowed origin can read the
value through their own scripts. Same-user CDP access can also read it.

The broker suppresses secret-fill results, removes the worker's `DEBUG`
environment variable and scrubs known values from model text and diagnostics.
These measures do not make browser content or exported artifacts safe to share.
No credential manager, secret creation or automatic recording is enabled.
Recording requires explicit opt-in and stores files in the workspace.

## Supported versions

Security fixes are provided for the latest published release. Reports against
older versions should first be reproduced on the latest version when possible.
